081.json.summary: Markandeya begins to tell how Savarni, son of the Sun, became the eighth Manu through the power of the Great Illusion (Mahamaya). Long ago, in the age of Svarochisha Manu, there was a king named Suratha of the Chaitra line who ruled the whole earth and cared for his people like his own children. Enemy kings, the Kolavidhvamsis, defeated him in battle, and back in his own city his strong and wicked ministers took his treasury and army. On the excuse of hunting he rode alone into a deep forest and came to the peaceful hermitage of the sage Medhas, where even wild beasts were calm. Living there, he kept worrying about his lost city, his favourite elephant, his servants now serving other kings, and his treasury being wasted. Near the hermitage he met a merchant (vaishya) named Samadhi, born in a rich family, who had been driven out by his greedy wife and sons, who took his wealth; yet he still worried whether they were well and could not make his mind hard against them. The two went to the sage, and the king asked why both of them, though they knew better, still felt attachment to those who had hurt them. The sage said all creatures have knowledge of objects, even birds and beasts; birds feed their young though hungry themselves, and people want sons hoping for return; yet all are thrown into the whirlpool of 'mine' by Mahamaya, the yoga-sleep of Vishnu, who forcibly pulls even the minds of the wise into delusion. She creates the world; when pleased she grants freedom; she is both the highest knowledge that frees and the cause of bondage. Asked who she is, the sage says she is eternal, the world is her form, but she is said to be 'born' whenever she appears to help the gods. At the end of an age, when Vishnu slept on the serpent Shesha in the single ocean, two demons born from the wax of his ears, Madhu and Kaitabha, rose to kill Brahma, who sat on the lotus from Vishnu's navel. Brahma praised the Yoga-sleep: she is Svaha and Svadha, the syllables and the half syllable beyond speech, Savitri, the creator, keeper and destroyer of the world, the great knowledge, great illusion, great memory, Prakriti of the three qualities, the dark Night of destruction, Shri, modesty, peace and patience, armed with sword, trident, club, discus, conch and bow, more beautiful than all beautiful things; since she made even Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma take bodies, no one can praise her fully. He asked her to confuse the two demons and wake Vishnu. She came out of Vishnu's eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart and chest and stood before Brahma; Vishnu woke and fought the two with his arms for five thousand years. Deluded by Mahamaya, the proud demons offered him a boon; he asked that they be killed by him. Seeing the whole world covered with water, they asked to be killed where the earth was not flooded, and Vishnu cut off their heads with his discus on his thigh. So she appeared when praised by Brahma, and the sage says he will tell more of her power.

082.json.summary: The sage (Medhas) tells how, long ago, the gods and the demons fought for a full hundred years, with Mahisha leading the demons and Indra the gods. The demons won, and Mahishasura became Indra himself. The defeated gods, led by Brahma, went to Shiva and Vishnu and told them how Mahisha had taken over the duties of the Sun, Indra, Agni, Vayu, the Moon, Yama, Varuna and the others, and had driven the gods out of heaven to wander the earth like mortals; they asked for a way to kill him. Hearing this, Vishnu and Shiva frowned in anger, and a great light (tejas) came out of the faces of Vishnu, Brahma and Shiva and the bodies of Indra and the other gods. It joined into one blazing mass like a mountain and became a woman whose light filled the three worlds. Shiva's light became her face, Yama's her hair, Vishnu's her arms, the Moon's her breasts, Indra's her waist, Varuna's her legs and thighs, Earth's her hips, Brahma's her feet, the Sun's her toes, the Vasus' her fingers, Kubera's her nose, Prajapati's her teeth, Agni's her three eyes, the two twilights' her brows and Vayu's her ears. The gods gave her their weapons: Shiva a trident, Vishnu a discus, Varuna a conch, Agni a spear, Vayu a bow and quivers, Indra a thunderbolt and a bell from his elephant Airavata, Yama a staff, Varuna a noose, Brahma a rosary and water pot, the Sun his rays, Time a sword and shield, the Milk Ocean a necklace, clothes and ornaments, Vishvakarma an axe and armour, the ocean lotus garlands, the Himalaya a lion to ride and jewels, Kubera a cup full of wine, and Shesha a serpent necklace. Honoured with these, she roared and laughed again and again; the worlds shook, the seas trembled and the mountains moved, while the gods cried 'Victory' and the sages praised her. The demons armed themselves, and Mahishasura ran towards the sound and saw the goddess filling the three worlds, her feet pressing the earth, her crown touching the sky, her thousand arms covering all directions. The battle began. Mahisha's general Chikshura, Chamara, Udagra, Mahahanu, Asiloma, Bashkala, Ugradarshana, Bidalaksha, Kala and others fought her with vast numbers of chariots, elephants and horses, and Mahisha himself with countless thousands. She cut their weapons easily and rained her own on them; her lion moved through the army like fire through a forest; from her breath came hundreds of thousands of attendants (ganas) who fought and played drums and conches. With trident, club, spear, sword, bell and noose she cut, crushed and pierced the demons; headless bodies rose and kept fighting or danced to the music, rivers of blood flowed, and in a moment Ambika destroyed the great army as fire burns a heap of grass and wood, while the gods rained flowers from the sky.

083.json.summary: The sage tells King Suratha how Mahishasura himself was killed. Seeing his army being destroyed, the general Chikshura attacked Ambika with a rain of arrows; she cut them easily, killed his horses and charioteer, broke his bow and banner and wounded him. He ran at her with sword and shield, struck the lion on the head and the goddess on her left arm, but his sword shattered; his blazing trident, thrown at Bhadrakali, she broke into a hundred pieces with her own trident and killed him. Chamara came on an elephant; his spear fell powerless at her shout of 'hum', she cut his trident with arrows, and the lion leapt onto the elephant, wrestled with him and tore off his head. Udagra was killed with stones and trees, Karala with teeth and fists; she crushed Uddhata with her club, killed Bashkala with a dart, Tamra and Andhaka with arrows, Ugrasya, Ugravirya and Mahahanu with her trident, Bidala with her sword, Durdhara and Durmukha with arrows, Kala with the staff of death, and Ugradarshana and Asiloma with her sword. As his army was wiped out, Mahishasura took his buffalo form and scattered her attendants with his muzzle, hooves, tail, horns, roar and breath, then rushed to kill her lion. In his rage the earth cracked under his hooves, his tail made the ocean flood, his horns tore the clouds and mountains fell from the sky at his breath. Chandika threw her noose and bound him; he left the buffalo form and became a lion; as she cut its head he became a man with a sword; she shot him down and he became a great elephant that dragged her lion with its trunk; she cut off the trunk, and he became a buffalo again and shook the three worlds. Angry, the Mother of the world drank the finest drink again and again and laughed with red eyes, while he roared and hurled mountains with his horns, which she smashed with arrows. She said: 'Roar, roar for a moment, fool, while I drink this honey; when I have killed you here the gods will soon roar.' She leapt onto him, pressed his neck with her foot and struck him with her trident; half-emerged from his own mouth and held by her power, he still fought, and she cut off his head with her great sword and threw him down. So Mahisha, with his army and friends, was destroyed; all beings cried 'Victory', the demon army fled crying, the gods rejoiced and praised her with the great sages, the gandharvas sang and the apsaras danced.

084.json.summary: After Mahishasura is killed, Indra and the gods, bowing low with joy, praise the goddess (this hymn is often called the Shakrādi Stuti). She spreads through the world by her own power and is the united power of all the gods; even Vishnu, Brahma and Shiva cannot describe her strength. She is fortune (Shri) in the homes of the good and misfortune in the homes of the wicked, intelligence in the wise, faith in the good and modesty in the well born. Though made of the three qualities, she is the cause of all worlds, unknown even to Vishnu and Shiva, the first and highest Nature (Prakriti). She is Svaha, by which the gods are fed in sacrifices, and Svadha, by which the ancestors are fed; she is the highest knowledge practised by sages seeking freedom, the three Vedas, the means of living (varta), wisdom (Medha), Durga the boat across the hard ocean of worldly life, Shri who lives in Vishnu's heart, and Gauri who lives with Shiva. The gods marvel that Mahisha, seeing her lovely moon-like face, still struck it, and that seeing her face angry he did not die at once. Those she favours are honoured, wealthy, famous and righteous; when remembered she removes fear and gives good thoughts; she removes poverty, pain and fear. She kills the wicked so the world may be happy and so that they, dying in battle, go to heaven instead of hell; that is why she uses weapons instead of burning them with a look; even with enemies her mercy is shown. They ask her to protect them with her trident, sword, bell and the twang of her bow, in the east, west, south and north, with her gentle and her fearful forms and all the weapons in her hands. Worshipped with flowers from the Nandana garden, perfumes and incense, the goddess, pleased, offers the gods a boon. They say all is done since their enemy is dead, but ask that whenever they remember her she will remove their great troubles, and that she will be pleased with any mortal who praises her with these hymns and increase his wealth, family and fortune. Saying 'So be it', Bhadrakali vanished. The sage says he has told how she arose from the bodies of the gods, and will now tell how she arose again from the body of Gauri to kill the wicked demons Shumbha and Nishumbha and to protect the worlds.

085.json.summary: The sage tells how, long ago, the proud and mighty demons Shumbha and Nishumbha took the three worlds and the sacrificial shares from Indra, and took over the offices of the Sun, Moon, Kubera, Yama, Varuna, Vayu and Agni, driving the gods out. Remembering the goddess's promise to destroy their troubles whenever they called on her, the gods went to the Himalaya and praised Vishnu's Maya. Their hymn bows again and again to the goddess, the great goddess, Shiva's consort, Nature, the gentle one, the fierce one, Gauri, the support of the world, Durga who takes one across difficulties, the very gentle and the very fierce; then, in its famous refrain, it bows 'to her, to her, to her, again and again' as the goddess who is present in all beings as Vishnu's Maya, as consciousness, intelligence, sleep, hunger, shadow, power, thirst, patience, birth, modesty, peace, faith, beauty, fortune, steadiness, livelihood, memory, compassion, right conduct, contentment, nourishment, mother and error, who rules the senses and pervades all beings, and who fills the whole world as pure consciousness. They ask her to bring them good and destroy their troubles. While they were praising, Parvati came to bathe in the Ganga and asked whom they were praising; from the sheath of her body came the auspicious goddess, who said the hymn was for her, sung by the gods driven out by Shumbha and defeated by Nishumbha. Because she came out of Parvati's body-sheath (kosha) she is called Kaushiki, and Parvati, left dark, became Kalika, living in the Himalaya. Chanda and Munda, servants of Shumbha and Nishumbha, saw Ambika in her most beautiful form and told Shumbha that a woman lighting up the Himalaya, a jewel among women, was there; since he already owned all the jewels of the three worlds (Indra's elephant Airavata, the Parijata tree, the horse Uchchaihshravas, Brahma's swan chariot, Kubera's treasure, Varuna's umbrella and noose, Death's spear, clothes purified by Agni and more), why should he not take her too? Shumbha sent the messenger Sugriva, who told her sweetly that Shumbha, lord of the three worlds, who enjoys all the best things, invited her to marry him or his brother Nishumbha and gain great wealth. Smiling, the goddess said this was true, but she had once foolishly made a vow: only one who beats her in battle, removes her pride and equals her in strength will be her husband; so let Shumbha or Nishumbha come, defeat her and take her hand. The messenger called her proud: how could a single woman face those whom Indra and all the gods could not, and warned that she would be dragged by the hair. She answered that they are indeed strong, but her vow was made without thought and cannot be broken; let him report her words to the demon king and let him do what is right.

086.json.summary: The angry messenger told the demon king everything the goddess had said. Shumbha in a rage ordered the demon chief Dhumralochana to take his army and bring her by force, dragging her by the hair, and to kill anyone, god, yaksha or gandharva, who tried to protect her. Dhumralochana went quickly with sixty thousand demons, saw the goddess on the snowy mountain and shouted that she must come to Shumbha and Nishumbha willingly or he would drag her there by the hair. The goddess said that if he, a strong warrior sent by the demon king with an army, takes her by force, what can she do to him? He rushed at her, and Ambika burned him to ashes with just the sound 'hum'. She then showered the angry demon army with sharp arrows, spears and axes, and her lion, shaking its mane and roaring fearfully, fell on the army, killing demons with blows of its paws, with its mouth and by trampling them, tearing open their bellies with its claws, cutting off heads and arms, and drinking blood; in a moment the whole army was destroyed. Hearing that Dhumralochana and his army had been killed by the goddess and her lion, Shumbha, his lip trembling with anger, ordered the great demons Chanda and Munda to go with a large army and bring her quickly, by the hair or bound; and if there was any doubt in the fight, to kill her and her lion with all their weapons, then come back.

087.json.summary: Ordered by Shumbha, the demons led by Chanda and Munda marched with a full army of four divisions and saw the goddess smiling, seated on her lion on a great golden peak of the Himalaya. When they tried to seize her, some with drawn bows and swords, Ambika grew very angry and her face turned black as ink. From her frowning forehead came Kali, with a terrible face, holding a sword and noose and a strange skull-topped staff (khatvanga), wearing a garland of human heads and a tiger skin, dreadful with dried flesh, with a huge mouth, lolling tongue, sunken red eyes and a roar that filled all directions. She fell on the demon army and ate it: with one hand she threw elephants into her mouth with their riders and bells, and chewed up warriors with their horses and chariots with their drivers; she seized some by the hair or neck, trampled others and crushed others with her chest; she caught their weapons in her mouth and ground them with her teeth. In a moment the army was destroyed. Chanda covered her with terrible arrows and Munda hurled thousands of discuses, which entering her mouth looked like many suns entering a cloud. Kali laughed fearfully, mounted her great lion, ran at Chanda, seized him by the hair and cut off his head with her sword; Munda rushed at her and she struck him down too, and the rest of the army fled in fear. Kali took the heads of Chanda and Munda to Chandika and said with loud laughter: 'I have brought you these two great beasts as an offering in the sacrifice of battle; Shumbha and Nishumbha you will kill yourself.' Chandika said that since she had brought Chanda and Munda, she will be famous in the world as Chamunda.

088.json.summary: After Chanda and Munda were killed and much of his army destroyed, Shumbha in a rage ordered all his forces out: the eighty-six Udayudha chiefs, the eighty-four Kambus, fifty clans of Kotiviryas, a hundred clans of Dhaumras, and the Kalakas, Daurhridas, Mauryas and Kalakeyas; he himself marched out with many thousands. Chandika filled earth and sky with the twang of her bow, the lion roared, Ambika rang her bell, and Kali, opening her mouth wide, roared louder still; the angry demons surrounded them on all sides. Then, for the destruction of the demons and the good of the gods, the powers (shaktis) of Brahma, Shiva, Skanda, Vishnu and Indra came out of their bodies in the same form, ornaments and mounts as their gods: Brahmani on a swan chariot with rosary and water pot, Maheshvari on a bull with trident, snake bracelets and the crescent moon, Kaumari on a peacock with a spear, Vaishnavi on Garuda with conch, discus, club, bow and sword, Varahi in the boar form, Narasimhi in the man-lion form scattering the stars with her mane, and Aindri on the king of elephants with the thunderbolt and a thousand eyes. Shiva, surrounded by them, told Chandika to kill the demons quickly. From the goddess's body came the fierce power of Chandika, howling like a hundred jackals, who sent Shiva himself as her messenger to tell Shumbha and Nishumbha: let Indra have the three worlds and the gods their offerings, and go to the underworld if you want to live; if you want battle, come and let my jackals feed on your flesh. Because she sent Shiva as messenger she is known as Shivaduti. The angry demons attacked Katyayani with arrows and spears; she cut them with her arrows, while Kali tore enemies with her trident and staff, Brahmani robbed them of strength by sprinkling water from her pot, Maheshvari, Vaishnavi, Kaumari and Aindri killed them with trident, discus, spear and thunderbolt, Varahi with snout, tusks and discus, Narasimhi with her claws, and Shivaduti with her laughter, eating those who fell. As the demons fled, the great demon Raktabija came to fight: from every drop of his blood that fell on the ground rose a demon as large as he was. When Aindri struck him with her thunderbolt, warriors like him rose from his blood; when Vaishnavi's discus, Kaumari's spear, Varahi's sword and Maheshvari's trident struck him, thousands more filled the world, and the gods were terrified. Chandika told Kali (Chamunda) to open her mouth wide, catch the blood and eat the demons born from it, so that Raktabija would run out of blood. The goddess struck him with her trident while Kali drank his blood; his club did not even hurt Chandika; Chamunda ate the demons that sprang up in her mouth, and the goddess killed the bloodless Raktabija with trident, discus, arrows and swords. The gods were overjoyed and the band of Mothers danced, drunk with blood.

089.json.summary: King Suratha asks what Shumbha and the very angry Nishumbha did after Raktabija was killed. The sage says both were furious; Nishumbha rushed at the goddess with the best of the demon army, and Shumbha came too with his forces. Shumbha and Nishumbha fought her, raining arrows like two clouds; Chandika cut their arrows and wounded them. Nishumbha struck her lion on the head with sword and shield (the text repeats this verse twice); when she cut his sword and shield, he threw a spear, which she split with her discus; his trident she crushed with her fist, his club her trident burned to ashes, and as he came with an axe she brought him down with arrows. Seeing his brother fall, Shumbha came in his chariot with eight huge arms holding weapons, filling the sky. The goddess blew her conch, twanged her bow and rang her bell, which destroyed the strength of the demons; the lion roared, Kali leapt up and struck the earth with her hands, and Shivaduti laughed fearfully, so that the demons trembled. When Ambika said 'Stop, wicked one', the gods in the sky cried 'Victory'. Shumbha's flaming spear she struck down with a great fiery missile; their arrows cut each other by hundreds and thousands; then she struck Shumbha with her trident and he fell unconscious. Nishumbha recovered, shot at the goddess, Kali and the lion, made ten thousand arms and covered Chandika with discuses; Durga cut them all. He ran at her with a club, which she cut with her sword, then with a trident; she pierced his heart with her trident, and out of his heart came another mighty man crying 'Stop!'; laughing, she cut off his head and he fell. The lion ate demons, crushing their necks with its teeth, as did Kali and Shivaduti; others were killed by Kaumari's spear, driven off by Brahmani's water purified with mantras, pierced by Maheshvari's trident, crushed by Varahi's snout, cut to pieces by Vaishnavi's discus and struck by Aindri's thunderbolt; some died, some fled the battle, and others were eaten by Kali, Shivaduti and the lion.

090.json.summary: Seeing his brother Nishumbha, dear to him as life, killed and his army being destroyed, Shumbha angrily told Durga not to be proud, since she fought relying on the strength of others. The goddess said: 'I alone exist in this world; who else is there besides me? See, wicked one, these powers of mine are entering into me.' Brahmani and all the other goddesses then merged into her body, and Ambika alone remained; she said that she had stood there in many forms through her power, but had now withdrawn them and stood alone, and told him to stand firm. A terrible fight followed between the goddess and Shumbha, watched by gods and demons, with arrows, weapons and divine missiles; she broke his missiles easily with sounds like 'hum'. When he covered her with hundreds of arrows, she cut his bow; she cut the spear in his hand with her discus; as he ran at her with a sword and a shield shining with a hundred moons, she cut both, killed his horses and charioteer and broke his chariot; she cut his iron club with arrows. He still rushed at her with his fist raised and struck her on the chest; she slapped him on the chest and he fell, but rose again, seized her and leapt up into the sky, where she fought him without any support. They wrestled in the sky for a long time, amazing the siddhas and sages; then Ambika lifted him, whirled him round and threw him to the ground. He jumped up and ran at her with his fist raised to kill her, and the goddess pierced his chest with her trident and threw him down. He fell dead, shaking the whole earth with its oceans, islands and mountains. When the wicked one was dead the whole world became calm and well, the sky became clear, the clouds of bad omen and the meteors stopped, the rivers flowed in their courses, the gods were filled with joy, the gandharvas sang sweetly, others played music and the apsaras danced, pure winds blew, the sun shone brightly, and the sacred fires burned calmly. (The last verse is incomplete in this text.)

091.json.summary: When the great demon king was killed, the gods led by Agni and Indra, their faces bright with joy, praised Katyayani (this hymn is known as the Narayani Stuti). They ask the goddess, who removes the pain of those who come to her, to be pleased and protect the world: she alone is its support as the earth and nourishes it as water; she is Vishnu's power of endless strength, the seed of the world and the highest Maya, who deludes all and, when pleased, gives freedom; all forms of knowledge and all women in the world are parts of her. Each verse then ends 'O Narayani, salutation to you': to her who lives as intelligence in every heart and gives heaven and freedom, who brings change through the divisions of time, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the power of creation, keeping and destruction, the refuge of the helpless; and to her forms as Brahmani on the swan chariot sprinkling holy kusha water, Maheshvari with trident, moon and snake on a great bull, Kaumari with peacock, cock and spear, Vaishnavi with conch, discus, club and bow, Varahi lifting the earth on her tusk, Narasimhi, Aindri with crown and thunderbolt who took Vritra's life, Shivaduti with her great roar, and Chamunda with terrible teeth and a garland of heads; and to her as Lakshmi, modesty, great knowledge, faith, nourishment, Svadha, the great night, the great illusion, wisdom and Sarasvati, with hands, feet, eyes, heads and ears on every side. They pray to Durga to protect them from fear, and that her gentle three-eyed face, her flaming trident, her bell which destroys the demons' strength, and her sword smeared with demon blood protect them. When pleased she removes all disease, when angry she destroys all hopes; those who take refuge in her meet no disaster and become a refuge for others. Who but she could have destroyed the demons by making herself into many forms? She guards the world among demons, poisonous snakes, enemies, robbers, forest fires and the open sea. They ask her to protect them always, as she did now, and to remove the sins of the world and the great troubles caused by evil omens. The goddess offers a boon, and the gods ask that she always remove the troubles of the three worlds and destroy their enemies. She then foretells her future appearances: in the twenty-eighth age of the Vaivasvata period, when two other demons named Shumbha and Nishumbha are born, she will be born from Yashoda in the house of Nandagopa, live on the Vindhya mountain and kill them; in a very fierce form she will kill the Vaiprachitta demons and her teeth will become red as pomegranate flowers, so she will be called Raktadantika; after a hundred-year drought she will be born, not from a womb, and look on the sages with a hundred eyes, and be called Shatakshi; she will feed the world with life-giving vegetables grown from her own body until the rain comes and be called Shakambhari, and there she will kill the demon Durgama and be called Durga; taking a terrible form on the Himalaya she will eat demons to protect the sages and be called Bhima; and when the demon Aruna troubles the three worlds she will take the form of countless bees and kill him, and be called Bhramari. Whenever trouble arises from demons, she will come down and destroy the enemies.

092.json.summary: The goddess tells the gods the rewards of reciting her story. Whoever praises her daily with these hymns with a focused mind, she will free from all trouble. Those who recite with devotion the killing of Madhu and Kaitabha, of Mahishasura and of Shumbha and Nishumbha, on the eighth, ninth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, will have no sin or disaster from sin, no poverty, no separation from loved ones, and no fear from enemies, robbers, kings, weapons, fire or floods. So this story of her greatness should be read and heard with devotion; it calms all troubles from epidemics and the three kinds of evil omen. She will never leave the temple where it is properly recited daily; it should be recited at offerings, worship, fire rites and festivals, and she will accept with love worship and fire offerings made with or without knowledge. At the great yearly worship in autumn, one who hears it with devotion will by her grace be free of all trouble and gain wealth and grain. Hearing it, a man becomes fearless, enemies perish, good fortune comes and the family prospers. It should be heard in all rites for peace, after bad dreams and in severe troubles from the planets; troubles and planetary afflictions are calmed and bad dreams become good. It calms children seized by child-seizing spirits (bala-graha), brings friendship where people have fallen out, weakens all wicked people and destroys demons, ghosts and goblins just by being read. Hearing it once pleases her as much as a year of worship with animal offerings, flowers, water offerings, incense, perfumes, lamps, feeding Brahmins, gold and other gifts. Hearing the story of her births removes sins, gives health and protects from evil beings; hearing of her battles removes fear of enemies; the hymns of the gods, of the Brahmin sages and of Brahma give a good end. A person caught in a forest fire, surrounded by robbers in a lonely place, seized by enemies, chased by lions, tigers or wild elephants, sentenced to death or imprisoned by an angry king, tossed by wind on a ship at sea, under falling weapons in battle, or in any terrible trouble or pain, is freed by remembering her story, and lions, robbers and enemies run away. The sage says the fierce goddess Chandika then vanished before the gods' eyes; the gods, free of fear, took back their offices and their shares of sacrifice, and the surviving demons went to the underworld. Though eternal, she appears again and again to protect the world; she deludes the world and gives birth to it; when asked she gives knowledge and when pleased, prosperity. She fills the universe as Mahakali at the time of destruction; she is the great plague in time, and also creation and the keeping of beings; in good times she is Lakshmi bringing growth to the home, and in bad times misfortune (Alakshmi) bringing ruin. Praised and worshipped with flowers, incense and perfumes, she gives wealth, sons, a mind set on dharma and a good end.

093.json.summary: The sage ends the story of the goddess's greatness for King Suratha: such is the power of the goddess who upholds this world; by Vishnu's Maya the king, the merchant and other wise people are deluded, have been deluded and will be deluded. He tells the king to take refuge in this highest goddess, who when worshipped gives enjoyment, heaven and final freedom. Markandeya says that, hearing this, King Suratha, tired of his strong attachment and of the loss of his kingdom, bowed to the sage and went at once to do penance, and so did the merchant. To see the Mother, they stayed on a river bank, where the merchant chanted the highest hymn to the goddess (Devi Sukta). They made a clay image of the goddess on the river bank and worshipped it with flowers, incense, fire offerings and water offerings; fasting, with controlled and fixed minds, they also gave her offerings sprinkled with blood from their own bodies. After three years of such worship, Chandika, the upholder of the world, appeared before them pleased and offered whatever they wished. The king chose a kingdom that would not be lost in another life, and in this life his own kingdom back, won by force after destroying his enemies' power. The merchant, whose mind had turned away from the world, chose the knowledge that removes the attachment of 'mine' and 'I'. The goddess told the king that in a few days he would regain his kingdom by killing his enemies and it would stay secure; and that after death he would be born again from the Sun god (this verse is incomplete in the text). To the merchant she gave the knowledge he wanted, for his final success. Having given both their wishes, and praised by them with devotion, she vanished. So, having received the goddess's boon, Suratha, the best of kshatriyas, will be born from the Sun and become the Manu Savarni.
